title: Spaceflight & Altered Gravity
summary: Explore how microgravity and space radiation reshape fluids, bones, muscles, senses and the brain.

lessons.title: Fluid Shifts and Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome

levels.kid:
On Earth, gravity pulls the water in your body down toward your legs. In space, there is almost no pull. So the fluid floats up toward your chest and head.

Astronauts get puffy, round faces and skinny legs. People call this "puffy face, bird legs." Their noses feel stuffy, like having a cold.

The extra fluid near the head can also press gently on the back of the eyes. Over months, some astronauts' eyes change shape a little. Things up close can look blurry. Doctors call this **SANS**.

Scientists check astronauts' eyes with special cameras. They are testing tricks to pull fluid back down, like special pants that suck gently on the legs.
levels.hs:
On Earth, gravity creates a **hydrostatic gradient**: the pressure in your blood vessels is higher in your feet than in your head. Your body is built around this. In **microgravity**, that gradient disappears, and roughly 1.5 to 2 liters of fluid shift from the legs toward the chest and head. This is the **cephalad fluid shift** (cephalad means "toward the head").

Visible effects:
- Puffy face and swollen eyelids
- Thinner legs ("bird legs"), with leg volume dropping by about 10%
- Nasal stuffiness and headaches

The body senses extra blood in the chest and responds as if it has too much fluid. Within days, total plasma volume falls by about 10 to 15%.

On long missions, many astronauts develop **Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome (SANS)**. Its signs include swelling of the **optic disc** (where the optic nerve enters the eye), flattening of the back of the eyeball, folds in the layers behind the retina called **choroidal folds**, and a shift toward farsightedness. That shift is called a **hyperopic shift**.

A real example: in 2011, Mader and colleagues described seven astronauts who flew about six months on the International Space Station and came back with these eye changes. Some had them for years afterward. NASA now ranks SANS as a major risk for Mars missions.
levels.college:
**Mechanics of the fluid shift.** Standing on Earth, the column of blood gives a pressure difference of roughly 0.77 mmHg per cm of height. Feet sit near 90 to 100 mmHg above heart level, and the head is slightly negative. Removing gravity abolishes this gradient, and fluid redistributes headward within hours. Leg tissue loses interstitial fluid and blood volume. The face, neck veins and upper body gain both.

**Early physiological responses:**
- Central venous pressure, surprisingly, *falls* in flight. The chest expands and intrathoracic pressure drops, while transmural pressure across the heart wall rises. Cardiac filling and stroke volume increase early.
- Atrial stretch and volume sensing reduce thirst and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activity. Combined with fluid moving out of the vessels, plasma volume falls 10 to 17%, a new steady state reached within days.
- Jugular veins become distended, and some astronauts have shown stagnant or reversed jugular flow, with occasional **internal jugular vein thrombosis**.

**SANS findings** (more likely with longer flights, roughly half to two-thirds of long-duration crew show some sign):
- **Optic disc edema**, often asymmetric and milder than in terrestrial intracranial hypertension
- **Globe flattening** at the back of the eye
- **Choroidal folds** and thickening of the choroid, the vascular layer under the retina
- **Cotton wool spots**, small areas of retinal nerve-fiber injury
- **Hyperopic shift**, because a shorter eye focuses light behind the retina

**Leading hypothesis.** Without daily cycles of upright posture, the head never gets relief from venous and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) congestion. Mildly but constantly raised pressure in the head is transmitted along the optic nerve sheath to the back of the eye. The pressure difference across the lamina cribrosa, the mesh where optic nerve fibers leave the eye, may drive disc swelling.

Monitoring uses optical coherence tomography (OCT), fundus photography and ultrasound aboard the ISS.
levels.phd:
**The pressure problem.** SANS resembles idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), but astronauts rarely report the headaches, pulsatile tinnitus or diplopia typical of IIH. Post-flight lumbar punctures (Mader 2011) showed opening pressures only mildly elevated, roughly 18 to 28.5 cmH2O, measured after landing. A key study using Ommaya reservoir patients in parabolic flight (Lawley et al., 2017) found that intracranial pressure (ICP) in acute weightlessness was *lower* than supine on Earth but *higher* than upright seated. This is the core insight: microgravity does not produce pathological ICP. It removes the daily low-pressure periods of upright posture, giving a chronically "supine-like" load that is never relieved.

**Translaminar pressure difference.** Optic disc health depends on intraocular pressure minus retrolaminar (optic nerve subarachnoid) pressure. Modest persistent rises in retrolaminar pressure, possibly worsened by CSF compartmentalized in the optic nerve sheath, could reverse the normal gradient. This would explain disc edema with only modest ICP. Asymmetric findings support local sheath anatomy, a "compartment syndrome" variant.

**Brain imaging.** Roberts et al. (2017, NEJM) found upward brain shift, narrowing of the central sulcus and crowding at the vertex after long flights. Lateral ventricles enlarge by roughly 10 to 25%, and recovery is incomplete a year later. Glymphatic and perivascular space changes are being studied.

**Choroidal engorgement.** Venous congestion of the choroid, measured by OCT, thickens it. This may push on the globe and produce folds, independent of CSF changes.

**Individual susceptibility.** Zwart and Smith reported that astronauts with SANS had higher homocysteine-related metabolites and carried risk alleles in one-carbon metabolism genes (e.g., *MTRR* 66G, *SHMT1* 1420C). This suggests vascular sensitivity to congestion. Higher dietary sodium and ambient CO2 on the ISS (often 2,000 to 5,000 ppm, versus about 400 ppm outdoors) are candidate contributors, with mixed evidence.

**Controversy.** Fluid congestion and ICP, choroidal venous stasis and optic nerve sheath compartmentalization are not mutually exclusive. A unifying model remains unproven.
levels.expert:
**Ground analog.** Strict 6° head-down tilt bed rest (HDTBR) is the main Earth model. The 30-day VaPER study at DLR's :envihab (Laurie et al., 2019) produced optic disc edema and choroidal folds in some subjects. A notable twist: adding 0.5% CO2 did not worsen findings beyond those seen in a prior bed rest cohort. Bed rest did not reproduce globe flattening or the hyperopic shift well, so the analog is imperfect. Bed rest retains a gravity vector across the body, which flight lacks.

**Countermeasures under evaluation:**
- **Lower body negative pressure (LBNP)**: suction chambers or wearable trousers drawing fluid footward. Brief LBNP in flight reduces jugular cross-sectional area and choroidal congestion, but whether daily hours prevent SANS is unknown.
- **Venoconstrictive thigh cuffs** (Russian "Braslet") sequester blood in the legs. They are mainly an acute tool for symptoms.
- **Swimming goggles** that raise intraocular pressure slightly, aiming to restore the translaminar gradient. This is early-stage work.
- **B-vitamin supplementation** for genetically susceptible crew is being studied.
- **Short-arm centrifugation** as artificial gravity may be the most physiologic option, but it is costly and causes motion side effects.

**Clinical pitfalls.**
- Pre-flight baseline OCT is essential. Mild disc edema is easily missed on fundoscopy alone, and normal optic disc variants can mimic swelling.
- The hyperopic shift is often managed with "space anticipation glasses" with adjustable focus. Correction is not prevention.
- Retinal folds and globe flattening can persist for years post-flight, so long-term follow-up is required.
- Jugular thrombosis was detected incidentally on ISS ultrasound in 2019 to 2020, raising difficult questions about anticoagulating someone far from definitive care.

**Open questions.**
- Does SANS plateau or progress over a roughly 2.5-year Mars mission? No human has flown that long continuously. The record is about 437 days, set by Valeri Polyakov in the mid-1990s.
- Is ventricular enlargement functionally harmless, or a sign of altered CSF dynamics that could interact with radiation effects?
- Can noninvasive ICP estimation, such as optic nerve sheath diameter, tympanic membrane displacement or transcranial Doppler, be validated in flight?

For a neurosurgery-minded reader, SANS is a natural experiment in CSF physiology, venous outflow and optic nerve biomechanics, with direct parallels to IIH and shunt management.

keyPoints: Microgravity removes the hydrostatic gradient, shifting about 1.5-2 L of fluid toward the head
'Puffy face, bird legs' and nasal congestion appear within hours
Plasma volume falls about 10-15% as the body treats chest fullness as excess fluid
SANS: optic disc edema, globe flattening, choroidal folds, hyperopic shift
Key idea: no daily upright posture means intracranial pressure is never relieved
Countermeasures under study include lower body negative pressure and thigh cuffs

test.q: Why does body fluid move toward the head in microgravity?
choices: Cabin air pressure is lower than on Earth
The hydrostatic pressure gradient is lost
The heart pumps far harder in space
Kidneys stop filtering blood in orbit
test.explain: Gravity normally keeps more fluid in the legs. Without it, the gradient disappears and fluid redistributes headward.

test.q: What does the phrase 'puffy face, bird legs' describe?
choices: Bone loss in the lower limbs
An allergic reaction to cabin air
Muscle growth in the upper body
test.explain: Fluid leaves the legs and pools in the face and upper body.

test.q: How does plasma volume change in the first days of spaceflight?
test.explain: Sensing extra central volume, the body reduces thirst and hormone-driven fluid retention, so plasma volume drops.

test.q: Which change in vision is typical of SANS?
test.explain: Flattening of the back of the eye shortens it, so light focuses behind the retina, a shift toward farsightedness.

test.q: Swelling where the optic nerve enters the eye is called:
test.explain: Optic disc edema is a hallmark sign of SANS.

test.q: Choroidal folds occur in which part of the eye?
choices: The vessel layer under the retina
The colored muscle around the pupil
The clear dome at the front
test.explain: The choroid is the blood-vessel layer beneath the retina. It can thicken and fold in SANS.

test.q: Which tool is a main way to monitor SANS on the ISS?
test.explain: OCT images retinal and optic nerve layers in detail. Fundus photography and ultrasound are also used.

test.q: The leading explanation for SANS is that in space the head:
choices: Lacks the daily upright pressure drop
Loses its blood supply for hours
test.explain: Pressure is not extreme, but it does not drop as it does when we stand or sit on Earth.

test.q: Which countermeasure pulls fluid back toward the legs?
choices: Breathing pure oxygen through a mask
Drinking extra water with each meal
test.explain: LBNP applies suction around the lower body, drawing fluid footward.

test.q: The movement of fluid toward the head is called the ___ fluid shift.
test.explain: Cephalad means toward the head.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome?
test.explain: SANS is NASA's term for the eye and brain changes seen with long-duration flight.

test.q: Fluid shifts toward the head cause nasal ___ in astronauts.
test.explain: Fluid pooling in the face and head makes the nose feel stuffy, like a cold.

kidTest.q: Where does body fluid move in space?
kidTest.explain: Without gravity pulling it down, fluid floats up toward the chest and head.

kidTest.q: What do astronauts' legs look like in space?
kidTest.explain: Fluid leaves the legs, giving 'bird legs.'

kidTest.q: How can astronauts' noses feel in space?
kidTest.explain: Extra fluid in the head makes the nose stuffy.

kidTest.q: What might look blurry for some astronauts after months in space?
kidTest.explain: Eye shape changes can make close-up things blurry.

kidTest.q: Astronauts get a round, p _ _ _ _ face in space.
kidTest.explain: Fluid collects in the face, making it puffy.

advancedTest.q: Lawley et al. found ICP in weightlessness was lower than supine but higher than seated. What does this imply about SANS?
choices: SANS stems from acute severe intracranial hypertension during launch
Intracranial pressure is unrelated to optic disc changes in astronauts
Supine bed rest on Earth should produce more severe SANS than flight
Loss of daily low-pressure upright periods, not extreme ICP, drives risk
advancedTest.explain: Pressure is modest but never relieved. The cumulative load, not peak pressure, is the proposed driver.

advancedTest.q: Why can optic disc edema occur with only mildly raised intracranial pressure?
choices: Space radiation directly inflames the optic disc tissue
Plasma volume loss thickens the blood and blocks retinal arteries
Intraocular pressure rises sharply and pushes the disc outward
Optic nerve sheath CSF can alter the translaminar pressure difference
advancedTest.explain: Local retrolaminar pressure, possibly from compartmentalized sheath CSF, can reverse the gradient across the lamina cribrosa.

advancedTest.q: Astronauts with SANS carried variants in one-carbon metabolism genes. The best interpretation is:
choices: SANS is a single-gene inherited disease unrelated to flight
These genes directly control cerebrospinal fluid production rates
Genetic factors may set vascular susceptibility to fluid congestion
Those variants protect astronauts from optic disc swelling
advancedTest.explain: Flight provides the exposure, and genetics plus B-vitamin status may modify individual vulnerability.

advancedTest.q: Why is 6° head-down tilt bed rest an imperfect SANS analog?
choices: Subjects breathe pure oxygen, which masks eye changes
It produces far more severe disc edema than spaceflight does
A gravity vector persists, and globe flattening is poorly reproduced
It fails to shift any fluid toward the head
advancedTest.explain: Bed rest still has gravity acting across the body, and it reproduced disc edema and folds but not globe flattening or hyperopic shift well.

lessons.title: Bone Loss and Muscle Atrophy in Microgravity

levels.kid:
Your bones and muscles are like a team that gets stronger when it works. Every time you stand, walk or jump, gravity pushes on you, and your body says, "Better keep these bones and muscles strong!"

In space, astronauts float. Their legs barely have to hold them up. So the body thinks, "We don't need so much bone and muscle here," and it starts taking some away. Leg and back muscles shrink. Hip and spine bones get thinner, a bit like a sponge with bigger holes.

To fight this, astronauts exercise about two hours every day. They run on a treadmill while strapped down with bungee cords, and they lift on a special machine. Hard work keeps their bodies ready for coming home.
levels.hs:
On Earth, gravity constantly loads your skeleton and the muscles that hold you upright. These are called **weight-bearing** or **antigravity** structures: the hips, spine, thighs and calves. In **microgravity**, that load almost disappears, and the body adapts by removing tissue it no longer seems to need.

**Bone loss.** Bone is living tissue that is constantly remodeled. **Osteoclasts** break bone down and **osteoblasts** build it up. In space, breakdown speeds up while building lags behind. Without countermeasures, astronauts lose about 1-1.5% of hip and spine bone mineral density per month. That is roughly what an older woman after menopause loses in a year. The calcium released goes into the blood and urine, which raises the risk of **kidney stones**.

**Muscle atrophy.** Muscles shrink (**atrophy**) because protein breakdown outpaces protein building. The calf muscle (soleus) is hit hardest. Strength can fall even faster than size.

**Countermeasures.** On the International Space Station (ISS), crews exercise about 2 hours daily:
- **ARED** (Advanced Resistive Exercise Device), which uses vacuum cylinders to mimic weightlifting
- a treadmill with a harness that pulls the runner down
- a cycle ergometer

With ARED and good nutrition, crews now protect muscle well and lose much less bone. However, some bone loss still occurs, and it can take years to recover after landing.
levels.college:
Microgravity removes the two main mechanical signals to the musculoskeletal system: **ground reaction forces** (impact loading) and **postural muscle activity**. Tissues remodel toward the reduced demand.

**Bone: uncoupled remodeling**
- Resorption markers (urinary N-telopeptide, CTX) rise within days. Formation markers stay flat or fall, so remodeling becomes **uncoupled**.
- **Osteocytes** are the mechanosensors buried in bone. When unloaded, they increase **sclerostin**, which inhibits Wnt signaling and therefore osteoblast formation. They also raise **RANKL** relative to osteoprotegerin, which drives osteoclast activity.
- Losses are site-specific. Without countermeasures, hip and lumbar spine lose about 1-1.5% of areal BMD per month. **Trabecular** (spongy) bone suffers most. The skull may slightly gain bone, possibly because of headward fluid shifts.
- Released calcium raises urinary calcium. It also suppresses parathyroid hormone and active vitamin D, which reduces gut calcium absorption.

**Muscle: disuse atrophy**
- Antigravity muscles atrophy fastest: soleus, gastrocnemius, quadriceps and paraspinal muscles. Strength losses exceed volume losses, partly because of reduced neural drive.
- Protein synthesis falls (lower mTORC1 signaling). Breakdown rises through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (MuRF1, atrogin-1).
- Slow (type I) fibers in the soleus shift toward faster isoforms. Mitochondrial content also falls, which reduces aerobic capacity.

**Countermeasures**
- **ARED** (installed 2008) allows heavy resistance loads. Combined with treadmill running, cycling and adequate energy and vitamin D intake, it has markedly reduced bone and muscle losses.
- One flight study showed that adding a **bisphosphonate** (alendronate) to ARED largely prevented loss of hip BMD.

After return, muscle mass recovers over weeks to months. Bone recovers slowly, and bone structure may not fully return.
levels.phd:
**Mechanotransduction.** Osteocytes sense fluid-shear and strain through their lacunar-canalicular network. They use primary cilia, integrins, connexin-43 hemichannels and the mechanosensitive channel **Piezo1**. Unloading increases osteocyte expression of **SOST** (sclerostin), which antagonizes LRP5/6 and suppresses canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling in osteoblast lineages. Unloading also raises the **RANKL/OPG** ratio. In rodent hindlimb unloading (the Morey-Holton model), Sost knockout mice are protected from bone loss, which makes sclerostin a causal mediator.

**Quantitative skeletal data.** LeBlanc and colleagues used DXA on Mir crews and found monthly losses of about 1.0-1.6% at the hip and about 1% at the spine. Lang and colleagues used QCT and showed that trabecular hip loss reached about 2.2-2.7% per month. It exceeded cortical loss and reduced estimated femoral strength more than areal BMD suggested. HR-pQCT of the distal tibia after 4-6 month ISS missions shows trabecular and cortical deficits. These deficits are only partly restored a year after landing. Bone strength therefore recovers more slowly than density.

**Mineral metabolism.** Increased resorption raises serum ionized calcium, which suppresses PTH and 1,25(OH)2D3. Calciuria and supersaturation follow, which explains the **renal stone** risk. Studies by Smith and colleagues linked higher dietary sodium and animal protein, and lower energy intake, to greater resorption.

**Muscle molecular biology.** Unloading reduces IGF-1/Akt/mTORC1 signaling. It also frees FoxO transcription factors to induce the E3 ligases MuRF1 and atrogin-1/MAFbx. Calpain and autophagy pathways contribute as well. Fitts's biopsies from 6-month ISS crew showed soleus fiber volume and peak power falling substantially, even with pre-ARED exercise. Thin-filament density also fell, which shifted the fibers toward higher shortening velocity.

**Nuance and controversy.** The NASA Twins Study showed considerable individual variability, and crew members respond differently. Ground analogs (6° head-down tilt bed rest, dry immersion) reproduce atrophy well. However, they imperfectly reproduce bone, fluid and radiation interactions. Some argue that DXA areal BMD underestimates fracture-relevant change. Others argue that post-flight hip-structure deficits overstate long-term risk, because real-world fracture data in astronauts remain sparse.
levels.expert:
**Mission relevance.** The key exploration problem is not loss on the ISS but cumulative risk on long missions. A Mars mission involves months of transit, then landing on a 0.38 g surface, possibly while deconditioned and without medical support. A fragility fracture or a renal stone there could end the mission. NASA tracks this through formal risk records: Risk of Bone Fracture, Early-Onset Osteoporosis, and Renal Stone Formation.

**Monitoring pitfalls**
- **DXA areal BMD** misses compartment-specific trabecular and cortical change. It also misses geometric change. QCT-based **finite element analysis** of femoral strength gives better estimates of fracture load.
- Resorption markers respond fast but vary widely, and they depend on diet.
- Restored density on scans is not the same as restored architecture. Lost trabecular connectivity is largely irreversible.

**Countermeasure strategy**
- Exercise prescriptions emphasize high-load resistance and high-intensity intervals. In the SPRINT study, lower-volume, high-intensity training preserved muscle and VO2max comparably to traditional volume.
- Pharmacologic options under study include bisphosphonates (resorption suppression), denosumab (anti-RANKL; has rebound resorption on cessation, a real concern for timed missions) and romosozumab (anti-sclerostin, mechanistically ideal for unloading; carries a cardiovascular safety signal). Myostatin/activin blockade preserved muscle in mice flown on the ISS (Lee and colleagues, 2020).
- Nutrition is itself a countermeasure. Energy deficit accelerates both bone and muscle loss. Vitamin D repletion, controlled sodium and adequate protein matter.

**Clinical carryover.** Spaceflight is a compressed model of disuse osteoporosis and sarcopenia. It parallels spinal cord injury, prolonged ICU stays and immobilization after neurosurgery. Insights into sclerostin and resistive loading inform rehabilitation for these patients.

**Open questions**
- Is partial gravity (lunar 0.16 g, Martian 0.38 g) protective, and is there a dose-response threshold?
- How much do microgravity effects interact with radiation (which impairs osteoblasts) and elevated CO2?
- Could artificial gravity from short-arm centrifugation replace hours of daily exercise?
- Paraspinal muscle atrophy and intervertebral disc swelling correlate with post-flight disc herniation, which occurs at elevated rates. The mechanisms are unresolved.

keyPoints: Microgravity unloads antigravity bones and muscles, triggering disuse loss
Without countermeasures, hip and spine bone density falls about 1-1.5% per month
Unloaded osteocytes raise sclerostin and RANKL, uncoupling bone remodeling
Soleus and other postural muscles atrophy fastest; strength falls more than size
Bone-released calcium raises kidney stone risk
ARED resistance exercise, nutrition and possibly bisphosphonates protect astronauts

test.q: Without countermeasures, astronauts lose roughly how much hip bone density per month?
test.explain: Hip and spine lose about 1-1.5% per month, similar to a year of postmenopausal loss.

test.q: Which cell type breaks bone down?
test.explain: Osteoclasts resorb bone. Osteoblasts build it, and osteocytes sense load.

test.q: Which muscle is especially vulnerable to atrophy in microgravity?
test.explain: The soleus is a postural calf muscle that loses its constant antigravity work.

test.q: Why does spaceflight raise kidney stone risk?
test.explain: Calcium released from bone is excreted in urine, promoting stone formation.

test.q: What is ARED?
test.explain: The Advanced Resistive Exercise Device uses vacuum cylinders to mimic weightlifting.

test.q: Unloaded osteocytes increase sclerostin, which inhibits:
test.explain: Sclerostin blocks LRP5/6 and Wnt/β-catenin signaling, reducing bone formation.

test.q: Which bone compartment suffers most loss in space?
test.explain: Spongy trabecular bone remodels fastest and loses the most. The skull may even gain bone.

test.q: In disuse atrophy, strength compared with muscle size typically:
test.explain: Strength losses exceed volume losses, partly because of reduced neural drive.

test.q: After landing, which tissue recovers most slowly?
test.explain: Muscle recovers over weeks to months. Bone architecture may never fully recover.

test.q: What term describes muscle shrinking from disuse?
test.explain: Atrophy is the loss of muscle mass when protein breakdown exceeds synthesis.

test.q: When resorption rises but formation does not, bone remodeling is said to be ___.
test.explain: Normally breakdown and building are coupled. In space they separate.

test.q: Which drug class (example: alendronate) helped prevent hip bone loss with ARED?
test.explain: Bisphosphonates suppress osteoclast resorption.

kidTest.q: Why do astronauts' bones get thinner in space?
choices: Their bones carry almost no weight
The rocket launch shakes them hard
Their space food has little calcium
kidTest.explain: In weightlessness, bones barely have to hold up the body. So the body breaks down bone faster than it rebuilds it, removing bone it thinks it doesn't need.

kidTest.q: Which muscles shrink most in space?
kidTest.explain: Legs and back usually hold us up against gravity.

kidTest.q: How long do astronauts exercise each day?
kidTest.explain: About two hours daily helps protect bones and muscles.

kidTest.q: What keeps astronauts on the treadmill?
kidTest.explain: Bungee cords pull them down so they can run.

kidTest.q: Bones get thinner, like a s _ _ _ _ _ with bigger holes.
kidTest.explain: Spongy inner bone loses pieces and gets more holes.

advancedTest.q: Sost knockout mice resist hindlimb-unloading bone loss. This best supports:
choices: Osteoclasts as cells that are unaffected by unloading
Sclerostin as a causal mediator of unloading loss
Hindlimb unloading as a poor model of disuse
Calcium intake as the main driver of unloading loss
advancedTest.explain: Removing sclerostin blocks the loss, which implicates Wnt suppression causally.

advancedTest.q: Why might DXA underestimate fracture risk after flight?
choices: It measures muscle and not bone
It is designed for measuring the skull
It overcounts calcium in the urine
It misses trabecular and geometric changes
advancedTest.explain: Areal BMD averages compartments. QCT showed larger trabecular loss and greater strength reduction.

advancedTest.q: Why is denosumab problematic for a timed exploration mission?
choices: It blocks vitamin D absorption fully
advancedTest.explain: After denosumab stops, resorption rebounds, which is risky if supply ends mid-mission.

advancedTest.q: During flight, unloading raises serum calcium. The expected hormonal response is:
advancedTest.explain: In microgravity, increased bone resorption releases calcium into the blood. Raised calcium suppresses PTH, which in turn reduces renal activation of vitamin D (calcitriol).

lessons.title: Post-Flight Orthostatic Intolerance

levels.kid:
Imagine filling a water balloon and holding it upside down. The water rushes to the bottom. On Earth, gravity pulls your blood down toward your feet, too. Your heart and blood vessels work hard all day to push blood up to your brain.

In space, there is almost no pull. Blood floats up toward the chest and head. The body thinks it has too much fluid, so it gets rid of some. The heart also gets a little lazy because its job is easier.

When astronauts come home and stand up, gravity suddenly pulls blood down to their legs again. Not enough reaches the brain. They can feel dizzy or even faint. Their bodies need a few days to relearn how to fight gravity.
levels.hs:
**Orthostatic intolerance** means being unable to stay upright without symptoms like dizziness, a racing heart, blurry vision, or fainting (**syncope**). "Orthostatic" means "standing upright."

On Earth, standing up makes roughly half a liter of blood pool in your legs and belly. Your body reacts in seconds: pressure sensors called **baroreceptors** in the neck and chest notice the drop and tell your nervous system to speed up the heart and squeeze blood vessels. Blood pressure stays steady.

In **microgravity**, things change:
- Fluid shifts toward the head, and the body responds by getting rid of fluid. **Plasma volume** drops by roughly 10 to 15%.
- With less work to do, the heart can shrink slightly.
- The reflexes that defend blood pressure get out of practice.

After landing, many astronauts can't stand quietly for long. In a classic NASA study, about two-thirds of Space Shuttle astronauts could not finish a 10-minute stand test after landing. Women were affected more often than men.

To help, astronauts drink salt water and fluids before landing (**fluid loading**) and wear **compression garments** that squeeze the legs. They also exercise in space. Most recover within days, though longer missions may need more recovery time.
levels.college:
Post-flight **orthostatic intolerance (OI)** is the inability to maintain blood pressure and cerebral perfusion when upright after spaceflight. It presents as **presyncope** (lightheadedness, tunnel vision, nausea) or **syncope**, and it matters most at landing, when crews may need to leave a vehicle in an emergency.

**Why it happens: three converging problems**
- **Hypovolemia.** The headward fluid shift in microgravity distends central veins and the heart. The body reads this as fluid excess, and fluid also moves out of the vessels, so plasma volume falls about 10-17%. Total blood volume falls with it.
- **Cardiac remodeling.** With lower loading, left ventricular mass falls, and the ventricle becomes smaller and less compliant. On Starling's curve, a smaller, stiffer ventricle loses more **stroke volume** for a given drop in filling pressure.
- **Impaired vasoconstriction.** Upon standing, a critical defense is raising **total peripheral resistance** through sympathetic release of norepinephrine onto α1-adrenergic receptors. Astronauts who become presyncopal often show a blunted vasoconstrictor response.

**Baroreflex changes.** Carotid-cardiac (vagal) baroreflex gain is reduced after flight. Many affected astronauts still mount a large heart-rate increase but cannot raise resistance enough. The result is a drop in mean arterial pressure despite tachycardia.

**Who is at risk**
- Women more than men, in part because of smaller baseline vasoconstrictor reserve.
- Those with lower baseline peripheral resistance ("low resistors").
- Long-duration crews, because exercise countermeasures blunt but do not abolish deconditioning.

**Testing.** Common tests include tilt-table or stand tests with beat-to-beat blood pressure monitoring, plus **lower body negative pressure (LBNP)**, which pulls blood into the legs to simulate standing.

**Countermeasures.** Pre-landing oral salt-and-water loading, compression garments (the Russian **Kentavr** suit), in-flight aerobic and resistance exercise, and cooling during reentry.
levels.phd:
The canonical framework comes from Buckey et al. (1996), who stand-tested Shuttle astronauts. Roughly 64% could not complete a 10-min stand after flights of about 1-2 weeks. Fritsch-Yelle et al. then contrasted finishers and non-finishers. Both groups lost plasma volume similarly, so hypovolemia alone did not explain the difference. Instead, presyncopal astronauts had lower preflight total peripheral resistance and failed to raise norepinephrine and resistance adequately while standing. Finishers, by contrast, showed exaggerated noradrenergic vasoconstriction. Women were overrepresented among non-finishers (Waters et al., 2002).

**Cardiac mechanics.** Levine and colleagues measured ventricular pressure-volume relations in microgravity and in head-down-tilt bed rest. Unloading reduces LV mass by roughly 8-12% over weeks and shifts the end-diastolic pressure-volume curve, producing a smaller, stiffer chamber. Because the Frank-Starling relation is steep at low filling pressures, the orthostatic fall in central venous pressure produces a disproportionate drop in stroke volume. Paradoxically, central venous pressure is lower in flight than supine on Earth: chest expansion lowers intrathoracic pressure, and the heart's transmural filling pressure rises.

**Autonomic findings.** Microneurography on Neurolab (STS-90) showed that muscle sympathetic nerve activity is actually elevated in and after flight. So the failure is not simply central sympathetic withdrawal. Explanations include end-organ hyporesponsiveness, impaired α-adrenergic signal transduction, or limited vasoconstrictor reserve when baseline outflow is already high. Proposed contributors to reduced vascular responsiveness include vascular remodeling and increased nitric oxide signaling, extrapolated from hindlimb-unloaded rat studies.

**Duration paradox.** After long-duration ISS missions, the incidence of failed stand tests rose in older Mir/ISS data. Yet with modern high-intensity countermeasures, structured protocols report fewer severe events than Shuttle-era projections predicted. The lesson is that **countermeasure dose**, not flight duration alone, determines outcome.

**Open debates.** Researchers still argue over how much weight each factor carries: volume versus vascular versus cardiac atrophy. The answer likely differs across individuals, which argues for phenotyping crews before flight.
levels.expert:
Clinically, post-flight OI behaves like a reversible, acquired form of **orthostatic hypotension** and **orthostatic tachycardia**, with mixed phenotypes. That makes it a natural model for terrestrial conditions with similar physiology:
- **Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS)**, which also features hypovolemia and a small heart. Notably, Levine's group reported reduced cardiac size in POTS.
- Deconditioning after **prolonged bed rest**, including neurosurgical and ICU patients mobilized after long immobility.

**Pharmacology tested for astronauts**
- **Fludrocortisone** (a mineralocorticoid to expand volume) restored plasma volume in a Shuttle trial but did not reduce presyncope. This supports the view that volume is not the whole story.
- **Midodrine**, an α1-agonist prodrug (active metabolite desglymidodrine), addresses the vasoconstrictor deficit directly. Ground studies showed protection, but one flight study found interactions: combined with promethazine (given for motion sickness), it worsened orthostatic outcomes and caused adverse effects. This is a reminder that pharmacokinetics and drug interactions in flight are under-characterized.
- Practical takeaway: crews arrive with altered absorption, volume distribution, and receptor sensitivity. Drugs tested on the ground cannot simply be assumed to transfer to flight.

**Operational strategy.** Today the emphasis is prevention through exercise. Levine's protocol of graded endurance training with one-time saline infusion after bed rest returned orthostatic tolerance to baseline, an approach later translated to POTS rehabilitation. On the ISS, ARED resistance training and cycle and treadmill work preserve LV mass better than older programs did. Crews also use compression garments, fluid loading, and supine extraction after landing.

**Exploration-class problems.** Mars crews will land after months of transit, with no ground support, and must egress unaided in partial gravity (0.38 g). Open questions include:
- Whether partial gravity protects or merely delays deconditioning.
- Whether intermittent **artificial gravity** from a short-radius centrifuge, perhaps combined with exercise, provides enough orthostatic stimulus.
- The interaction with SANS-related fluid physiology.
- Individualized risk prediction using preflight resistance phenotype and LBNP tolerance.

**Pitfall.** Heart-rate response alone is misleading, because a large tachycardia can coexist with failing pressure. Beat-to-beat blood pressure and stroke volume are essential.

keyPoints: Orthostatic intolerance is failure to maintain blood pressure and brain perfusion when upright
Microgravity causes plasma volume loss of about 10-17% through headward fluid shift
Cardiac unloading produces a smaller, stiffer left ventricle and lower stroke volume when standing
The key discriminator is inadequate vasoconstriction (total peripheral resistance), not low heart rate
Women and low preflight resistors are at higher risk
Countermeasures: exercise, fluid loading, compression garments; midodrine has been studied

lessons.title: Space Motion Sickness and Vestibular Adaptation

levels.kid:
Inside each of your ears is a tiny balance kit. It has little loops filled with liquid and tiny stones that sit on soft hairs. When you tip your head, the stones slide and tell your brain which way is down.

In space, nothing falls, so the stones float. Your eyes say "I'm upright," but your ears say "I can't tell!" Your brain gets confused, a bit like reading in a bumpy car. Many astronauts feel sick, tired and dizzy for the first two or three days.

Then the brain learns new rules and the sick feeling goes away. When astronauts come back to Earth, the brain has to learn the old rules again, so they feel wobbly for a while.
levels.hs:
About **60 to 70%** of astronauts get **space motion sickness (SMS)** during their first days in orbit. Symptoms include headache, loss of appetite, sleepiness, pale skin, sweating, nausea and sometimes vomiting. It usually starts within hours of reaching orbit and fades in **2 to 4 days**.

The cause lies in the **vestibular system** of the inner ear:
- The **semicircular canals** sense head rotation.
- The **otolith organs** (utricle and saccule) contain tiny calcium carbonate crystals called **otoconia** that sense linear acceleration and gravity.

On Earth, gravity constantly pulls on the otoliths, so the brain knows where "down" is. In **microgravity**, the otoliths still sense movement but no longer report gravity. The leading explanation, **sensory conflict theory**, says sickness happens when signals from the eyes, inner ear and body don't match what the brain expects.

Head movements, especially tilting and nodding, make it worse, so new astronauts are told to move slowly and keep their heads still. Visual tricks also matter: floating "upside down" relative to a module can cause a sudden **visual reorientation illusion**.

After landing, astronauts face the reverse problem. Their brains have adapted to space, so they wobble, feel dizzy when turning, and may feel sick again. This readaptation usually takes days.
levels.college:
Space motion sickness belongs to **space adaptation syndrome**, the cluster of neurovestibular disturbances in early flight. Onset is typically within the first hours; symptoms peak around flight day 1 to 2 and usually resolve by day 3 to 4. Severity is scored on a scale from mild to severe, and vomiting can be abrupt with little warning.

**Mechanism.** The brain builds an **internal model** of how motor commands should change sensory input. In 1 g, a head pitch shifts the otoliths relative to gravity and also rotates the canals; the two signals agree. In microgravity:
- Otoliths still sense translation but lose their static gravity signal, so tilt and translation can no longer be told apart.
- Canal signals are unchanged, which creates **canal-otolith conflict** during pitch and roll movements.
- Vision and body-contact (proprioceptive) cues lose a shared "down."

The **sensory conflict / neural mismatch** model (Reason and Brand; Oman) holds that sickness scales with sustained mismatch between expected and actual input. The **otolith tilt-translation reinterpretation (OTTR)** hypothesis proposes that the brain resolves the conflict by reading all otolith signals as translation, not tilt.

**Adaptation and its cost.** As the internal model updates, symptoms fade, but the change becomes maladaptive on return. Post-flight effects include:
- Postural ataxia and wide-based gait
- Tilt-translation illusions during head movements and vehicle motion
- Impaired gaze stabilization and **dynamic visual acuity**
- Re-entry motion sickness

Readaptation of balance generally takes days to weeks and lasts longer after long missions.

**Countermeasures.** These include restricting head movement, rotating-chair or virtual-reality preflight training, and drugs. **Promethazine**, an H1 antihistamine with anticholinergic effects, is the standard in-flight treatment. Scopolamine-based products have also been used. Earlier tests of susceptibility on Earth predict SMS poorly.
levels.phd:
**Neural substrate.** Vestibular afferents project to the vestibular nuclei and cerebellum (nodulus/uvula, flocculus). There, **velocity storage** and internal models estimate gravity direction by fusing canal and otolith input (Merfeld, Angelaki). Nodulus/uvula Purkinje cells encode tilt versus translation, solving the ambiguity that Einstein's equivalence principle creates: a linear-acceleration sensor cannot tell gravity from acceleration alone. Without gravity, the canal-otolith fusion that normally solves this breaks down.

The emetic output pathway runs through the **nucleus tractus solitarius**, parabrachial nucleus and medullary central pattern generators. Histaminergic (H1) and muscarinic (M3/M5) receptors are involved, which explains why antihistamine and anticholinergic drugs work. 5-HT3 antagonists such as ondansetron work well for chemotherapy nausea but poorly for motion sickness, which fits with a vestibular rather than vagal-gut trigger.

**Classic evidence.**
- **Neurolab (STS-90, 1998)** and earlier Spacelab missions recorded altered ocular counter-roll and otolith-ocular reflexes in flight.
- Animal studies (Bion primates; rodents on Neurolab) showed transient changes in otolith afferent sensitivity and in hair cell synapse numbers, suggesting peripheral as well as central plasticity.
- Lackner and DiZio's rotating-room work showed that sensorimotor adaptation is specific to context.

**Theories in tension.** Sensory conflict theory is widely accepted but hard to test, because it is difficult to quantify "expected" signals. Riccio and Stoffregen's **postural instability theory** argues that sickness follows long periods of unstable posture control. The **fluid-shift hypothesis**, in which cephalad fluid changes inner-ear or intracranial pressure, has also been proposed. Most data favor a central mismatch account with possible peripheral contributions.

**Quantitative markers.** Post-flight computerized dynamic posturography, especially sensory organization test condition 5 (eyes closed, sway-referenced support), drops sharply on landing day. Recovery follows a roughly exponential curve with a time constant of days. Long-duration crews recover more slowly than shuttle crews.
levels.expert:
**Operational impact.** SMS is a scheduling hazard, not just a matter of comfort. Agencies avoid spacewalks (EVA) in the first days because vomiting inside a suit could be fatal. Critical tasks are kept off flight days 1 to 3. **Promethazine** is effective, but its sedation and slower reactions cause real problems, and its effect on adaptation rate is unclear. Some data suggest anticholinergic or antihistamine drugs may delay central compensation, a tradeoff also seen in terrestrial vestibular rehabilitation. Treatment is often given by intramuscular injection or suppository because vomiting limits oral routes.

**Landing as the hazard.** For Artemis and Mars missions, the key risk shifts to arrival. Crews may need to pilot a lander, egress, or operate on the lunar surface (1/6 g) or Mars (0.38 g) right after the gravity transition, with no ground team to help. Field tests of standing, walking and egressing soon after Soyuz landings, such as NASA's Field Test study, showed significant early impairment followed by fast partial recovery. These results guide timing for post-landing tasks. Sensorimotor deficits combine with orthostatic intolerance in ways that are hard to separate in the field.

**Brain imaging.** MRI studies (Roberts; Koppelmans; Van Ombergen) found upward shifts of the brain and changes in vestibular cortex and cerebellar connectivity after flight. Some functional changes correlate with balance recovery, though separating fluid-shift artifacts from true plasticity remains difficult.

**Emerging countermeasures.**
- **Galvanic vestibular stimulation** for preflight adaptation training and possibly in-flight retuning
- Virtual-reality sensorimotor conditioning and **dual adaptation** training, where repeated exposure to two environments lets the brain switch between them
- Short-radius centrifuge **artificial gravity**, which brings its own Coriolis cross-coupling problem: head turns while rotating create strong canal illusions unless adapted gradually

**Open questions.** How well do adaptations stored after a first flight carry over, given that repeat flyers often have milder SMS? Do partial-gravity settings need their own adaptation states? Can individual susceptibility be predicted better than by vestibular tests on Earth? Clinicians treating vestibular disorders benefit from this work, because astronauts are a model of rapid, reversible vestibular deafferentation-like change.

keyPoints: About 60-70% of astronauts get space motion sickness, usually resolving within 2-4 days
Otoliths sense gravity and linear acceleration; semicircular canals sense rotation
In microgravity otoliths lose the gravity signal, creating sensory conflict
The brain updates its internal model, which then causes problems on return to Earth
Post-flight effects include ataxia, tilt-translation illusions and poor gaze stability
Promethazine treats SMS; EVAs and critical tasks are avoided in early flight days

lessons.title: Space Radiation and the Brain

levels.kid:
On Earth, we live under a giant invisible shield. Earth's magnetic field and thick air block most of the tiny, super-fast particles zooming through space. These particles are called **radiation**.

Astronauts on the space station still get some protection from Earth's magnetic field. But on a trip to Mars, they would leave that shield behind. Some space particles are like tiny bullets. They are heavy and fast enough to zip right through a spaceship wall and into the body, even the brain.

Scientists test this on mice. Mice hit with these particles sometimes had more trouble learning and remembering. So scientists are working on better shields, special medicines, and safer ways to travel far into space.
levels.hs:
Space travelers are exposed to **ionizing radiation**: particles with enough energy to knock electrons off atoms and damage molecules like DNA.

There are three main sources:
- **Galactic cosmic rays (GCR)**: particles from exploded stars far outside our solar system. They are mostly protons, but they also include heavy nuclei such as iron, called **HZE particles** (high charge, Z, and high energy).
- **Solar particle events**: bursts of mostly protons from the Sun during solar storms.
- **Trapped radiation** in Earth's Van Allen belts.

On Earth, the magnetic field and atmosphere block most of this. The International Space Station orbits inside much of the magnetic field's protection. A Mars mission would not.

HZE particles are a particular worry for the brain. As one passes through tissue, it leaves a dense track of damage, like a bullet rather than a spray of sand. Shielding is hard, because heavy particles hitting metal walls can break into showers of secondary particles.

In a real example, NASA-funded experiments at Brookhaven National Laboratory's **NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL)** beamed heavy ions at rodents. Exposed animals often showed poorer memory, attention and problem-solving, along with damaged connections between neurons. Scientists still debate how strongly these results apply to astronauts.
levels.college:
Space radiation is measured as **absorbed dose** (gray, Gy) and as **equivalent or effective dose** (sievert, Sv), which weights dose by how biologically damaging the radiation is. ISS crews receive very roughly 0.5-1 mSv per day. A round-trip Mars mission is estimated at around 1 Sv in total, mostly from GCR.

**Why HZE particles are special**
- Their **linear energy transfer (LET)** is high: they deposit a lot of energy per micrometer of path.
- Energy deposition is concentrated in a narrow core, with a halo of **delta rays** (secondary electrons) spreading outward.
- At typical mission fluences, a given neuron may be traversed by a heavy ion only rarely. But over a long mission, a meaningful fraction of cells would be hit at least once by some charged particle.

**Effects in the CNS (mostly from rodent studies)**
- **Oxidative stress**: reactive oxygen and nitrogen species damage lipids, proteins and DNA.
- **Neuroinflammation**: microglia become activated and release cytokines.
- **Dendritic changes**: fewer and simpler dendrites and dendritic spines in the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex.
- **Reduced neurogenesis** in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus.
- **Behavioral deficits**: impaired spatial memory, object recognition, attention set-shifting and fear extinction, sometimes after doses well below 1 Gy.

Unlike in cancer radiotherapy, where the brain receives large doses of mostly low-LET X-rays, space exposure is a low dose rate of mixed, partly high-LET particles. This makes clinical radiotherapy data only partly useful for predicting astronaut risk.

**Countermeasures**
- **Hydrogen-rich shielding** (polyethylene, water) fragments heavy ions with fewer secondaries than aluminum.
- Storm shelters protect against solar particle events.
- Candidate radioprotective compounds and antioxidants are being studied in research settings.
levels.phd:
Central nervous system (CNS) risk is one of NASA's major concerns for exploration-class missions. The worry is twofold: acute in-flight changes in behavior and cognition that could compromise operations, and late degenerative effects.

**Physics.** The GCR spectrum is roughly 87% protons, 12% helium nuclei and about 1% HZE nuclei. The HZE fraction contributes a disproportionate share of dose equivalent because quality factors rise steeply with LET. Track structure is central. An iron ion at 1 GeV/n has an LET of about 150 keV/µm, and its delta-ray penumbra extends for micrometers to millimeters. A single traversal can therefore affect cell bodies, dendrites and axons along a path through a whole circuit.

**Ground analogs.** Early NSRL work used single-ion beams, such as ⁵⁶Fe, ¹⁶O, ²⁸Si and ⁴⁸Ti. Since about 2018, the **GCR simulator** has delivered rapidly switched mixed-ion beams that better match spaceflight. A key limitation: exposures are usually given in minutes rather than spread over months, so they do not reproduce the true low dose rate.

**Mechanistic findings.**
- The Limoli group reported reduced dendritic complexity and spine density in medial prefrontal cortex after low-dose ¹⁶O and ⁴⁸Ti. These changes correlated with deficits in novel object recognition and fear extinction, and persisted for months.
- Synaptic proteins such as PSD-95 change, and long-term potentiation is altered.
- There are persistent microglial activation and complement-mediated synaptic pruning. Depleting microglia with a CSF1R inhibitor prevented some cognitive deficits in mice.
- Impaired adult hippocampal neurogenesis has been described.
- In transgenic Alzheimer's models, accelerated amyloid-β plaque deposition has been reported (Cherry et al., 2012).

**Nuance and controversy.**
- Results vary with sex, strain, age at exposure, ion type and task. Female mice are often more resistant on some measures.
- Dose-response curves are frequently non-linear, and some low doses produce larger effects than higher ones.
- Rodents are typically irradiated young, with a much shorter remaining lifespan than astronauts.
- Multiple-comparison problems and inconsistent replication have prompted calls for standardized behavioral batteries.

The translational gap between mouse behavior and human operational performance remains unresolved.
levels.expert:
**Defining an acceptable risk.** NASA does not yet have a quantitative permissible exposure limit for CNS effects comparable to its cancer limit. In 2022, NASA adopted a career effective-dose limit of 600 mSv, applied equally regardless of age or sex, but this limit is based on cancer risk. CNS risk is instead handled under its own risk category for adverse cognitive or behavioral conditions and is tracked through the Human Research Program's evidence reports. A Mars mission would likely exceed the career limit, which is part of why the standard is debated.

**Combined stressors.** Radiation does not act alone. Mission conditions also include fluid shifts, isolation and confinement, sleep restriction, raised ambient CO₂ and altered gravity. Combined-exposure studies, such as hindlimb unloading plus GCR, sometimes show non-additive interactions on neuroinflammation and behavior. Single-stressor dose limits may therefore misestimate risk.

**Human data are thin.**
- Apollo astronauts reported **light flashes**, thought to come from particles passing through the retina or visual pathway. This is the clearest human evidence of direct particle-nervous-system interaction.
- Cohort studies of astronaut mortality are small and confounded by the healthy-worker effect.
- The NASA Twins Study reported some post-flight declines in cognitive speed and accuracy, but this was a single subject in low Earth orbit, so radiation could not be separated from other factors.
- Ground analogs relevant to humans include proton and carbon-ion therapy cohorts. However, these involve high doses, are focal rather than whole-brain, and involve sick patients.

**Pitfalls when reading the literature.**
- Watch for acute high dose rates being presented as if they matched spaceflight.
- Be wary of rodent tasks with uncertain links to astronaut job demands.
- Small group sizes and possible publication bias make many effects uncertain.

**Emerging directions.**
- Validated touch-screen tasks that work in both rodents and humans.
- Biomarkers such as plasma neurofilament light and GFAP.
- Individual radiosensitivity profiling, which raises ethical concerns about crew selection.
- Protective approaches being explored include CSF1R-mediated microglial modulation, NOX2 inhibition, and extracellular vesicles from stem cells.

**Open questions** include whether exposure on a Mars mission meaningfully raises dementia risk, and whether the effects are reversible.

keyPoints: Space radiation comes from galactic cosmic rays, solar particle events and trapped belts
HZE particles (heavy, high-energy nuclei like iron) leave dense damage tracks
High linear energy transfer (LET) makes heavy ions especially damaging
Rodent studies show dendritic loss, neuroinflammation and memory deficits
Hydrogen-rich shielding works better than metal against heavy ions
Translating mouse data to astronauts remains uncertain

advancedTest.q: The biggest limitation of NSRL rodent exposures is that they:

Rely on human rather than animal subjects

advancedTest.q: Depleting microglia with a CSF1R inhibitor prevented some deficits. This implies:

Microglia physically block heavy-ion particle tracks
Microglial pruning causes part of the deficit
Neurons repair radiation damage by themselves

advancedTest.q: Why might single-stressor dose limits misestimate CNS risk?
choices: Radiation doses are measured too precisely
advancedTest.explain: Unloading, CO₂ and isolation can interact with radiation in non-additive ways, so limits based on radiation alone may be off.
